title: Samsung Refrigerator 5E Error Code: Causes and Fix
meta_description: 5E on a Samsung refrigerator is a defrost sensor fault. Sources split on which compartment, so check where the frost is before you buy a part.
h1: Samsung refrigerator 5E error code: what it means and how to fix it
answer: 5E means the control cannot get a believable reading from a defrost temperature sensor, so it does not know when to run or end a defrost cycle. The sensor is a small thermistor clipped to the evaporator coil behind a rear panel, and the fault is usually the sensor itself, its connector, or the wiring between them. Sources disagree about whether 5E refers to the fridge compartment sensor or the freezer one, and different model generations do not help, so rather than trusting either reading, look at where the frost is building: that tells you which coil to open up, and it takes a minute.
time_estimate: 1 hour to diagnose, plus 6 to 8 hours defrosting
safety_warning: Unplug the refrigerator at the wall before any panel comes off. The defrost heater behind the evaporator cover runs at mains voltage and its wiring sits right alongside the sensor you are checking. The sealed refrigerant circuit, meaning the compressor, the coils and every pipe between them, is licensed-technician work: venting refrigerant is illegal and recharging needs certification and equipment you will not have at home. Never chip frost off a coil with anything metal.

causes.cause: The defrost sensor thermistor has failed
causes.confirm: Unplug the fridge, get the rear panel off the affected compartment and find the small bead sensor clipped to the coil. Measure across its two wires cold, then warm it in your hand and measure again. A thermistor reading that does not change, or that reads open or shorted, condemns it with no reference chart needed.

causes.cause: The sensor connector has corroded or worked loose
causes.confirm: The sensor measures correctly at its own leads but the code persists. Look at the plug for green corrosion, a pin backed out of its housing, or a wire pulled from its crimp. This area goes through a wet-dry cycle every defrost, so corroded connectors here are routine rather than unusual.

causes.cause: The coil is buried in ice because defrost has not been running
causes.confirm: Behind the rear panel the evaporator is a solid block of ice rather than lightly frosted. This is the consequence of the fault rather than the cause, but it has to be cleared before anything works again, and how much ice there is tells you how long the sensor has been dead.

causes.cause: Damaged wiring between the sensor and the board
causes.confirm: The sensor reads correctly at its own leads but gives a different answer measured at the board end. Follow the harness where it passes through the liner and where it crosses a metal edge, and flex it gently while watching the meter for a reading that jumps.

causes.cause: The defrost heater has failed as well
causes.confirm: A sensor that measures fine and a coil that still ices up. The sensor tells the control when to defrost; the heater does the defrosting. If the sensor checks out, measure the heater for continuity while you have the panel off, because you are already there.

A new sensor, a clean connector and a harness that measures through from the board end, and 5E still appears after a reset. The board reads this circuit, so it is the last suspect and much the dearest. Confirm the sensor twice before accepting it.

steps.name: Work out which compartment is in trouble
steps.detail: Feel both compartments and note which is not holding temperature. Then look for where frost is building: the back wall of the freezer, the back wall of the fridge section, or around a vent. Because the published descriptions of 5E disagree about which sensor it refers to, this observation is worth more than the code and decides which panel you take off.

steps.name: Photograph the display and check the characters
steps.detail: Zoom in on a photo of the panel. On these displays a 5 and a capital S are the same glyph, so 5E and SE are one code and both will appear in searches. Make sure you are not reading a 5C from a newer model either, since Samsung changed the suffix from E to C partway through the range and the fault is the same.

steps.name: Unplug and empty the affected compartment
steps.detail: Pull the plug at the wall rather than switching off at the panel. Move the food to a cooler, take out the shelves and drawers in the compartment you identified, and put towels down along the front edge, because what comes off the coil has to go somewhere.
steps.warning: Unplug at the wall. The defrost heater behind the rear panel runs at mains voltage.

steps.name: Remove the rear panel and look at the coil
steps.detail: Take out the screws holding the rear interior panel, usually a mix of Phillips screws and plastic clips, and ease it away. Behind it sit the evaporator coil, the fan and the defrost heater. Light even frost is normal. A solid white block filling the fins means defrost has not been running and confirms you are in the right place.
steps.warning: Fridge unplugged. Do not pull on wiring looms while easing the panel off.

steps.name: Find the sensor and test it without a reference chart
steps.detail: The defrost sensor is a small bead or capsule clipped to the coil, often near the top, with two wires running to a nearby plug. Unplug it and measure across its own leads on ohms. Write the number down, then close your hand around the sensor for a minute and measure again. It is a thermistor, so the resistance should fall clearly as it warms. No change, open circuit or a dead short all condemn it.
steps.warning: Measure resistance on a dead circuit only, with the fridge unplugged.

steps.name: Check the heater while the panel is off
steps.detail: You are already in there, so measure across the defrost heater's terminals for continuity too. An open circuit means the heater has failed as well, which explains an iced coil even with a healthy sensor. Finding this now saves taking the same panel off twice, which is most of the work in this job.
steps.warning: Fridge unplugged. The heater is a mains-voltage component.

steps.name: Defrost fully before reassembling
steps.detail: Leave the fridge unplugged with the doors open and towels down for six to eight hours until every fin is clear. A hairdryer on low, kept moving and held well back, speeds it up. Never use a screwdriver, knife or scraper on the coil: the tubing is thin-walled, and puncturing it releases the refrigerant and ends the appliance.
steps.warning: No metal tools on the coil. A punctured refrigerant line cannot be fixed at home.

still_showing: If the sensor passes the warming test and its connector is clean, measure the same circuit from the board end before you conclude anything, because a sensor that is fine at its own leads and wrong at the board means the wiring in between, and that is a repair rather than a part. The useful trick for an intermittent is to leave the meter connected at the board end and flex the harness along its length, particularly where it passes through the liner: a reading that jumps as you move it has just located the fault for nothing. If the sensor is good and the harness measures through, the next thing worth testing while the panel is already off is the defrost heater, because a coil that keeps icing with a healthy sensor usually means the heater has failed rather than the sensor circuit. Those two parts sit inches apart and both are modest. Only when the sensor, the harness and the heater all check out does the control board become the answer, and that is the expensive end on a sealed appliance. Two boundaries worth being clear about. First, do not let the code number route you to a compartment: the published descriptions of 5E disagree about whether it is the fridge or the freezer sensor, so open the panel where the frost actually is and ignore the argument. Second, if both compartments are warm, the compressor is running continuously and the coil is not even getting cold, that is not a defrost sensor problem at all. That pattern points at the sealed refrigerant system, and that is licensed work. Venting refrigerant is illegal and recharging requires certification and equipment you will not have at home. On an older fridge a sealed-system quote is usually the point to price a replacement instead of a repair.
reset_procedure: Unplug the refrigerator at the wall for five minutes, then plug it back in. The control stores the fault, so 5E will keep showing after you have replaced the sensor until it is reset. Give it a full day afterwards and then look behind the rear panel again: a coil that is lightly frosted rather than icing up is what tells you the defrost cycle is running properly once more.
model_notes: Published descriptions of 5E disagree about which sensor it refers to. Several references call it the fridge compartment defrost sensor, others the freezer defrost sensor, and some pages contradict themselves between their own heading and body text. Rather than pick one, go by where the frost is. Samsung also changed the refrigerator code suffix from E to C partway through the range, so the same fault appears as 5C on newer models. Two display traps are worth knowing: on a seven-segment panel the numeral 5 and a capital S are the same glyph, so 5E and SE are one code, and 5E on a Samsung washing machine is an unrelated drain fault that shares nothing but the characters.

parts.name: Defrost temperature sensor
parts.note: Cheap part; the work is getting the rear panel off and defrosting first

parts.name: Defrost heater
parts.note: Test it while the panel is off, because getting back in there is most of the job

parts.name: Sensor wiring harness
parts.note: For a sensor that reads correctly at its leads but wrong at the board

parts.name: Main control board
parts.note: Last by elimination, after sensor, harness and heater all check out

when_to_call: Call someone if the sensor, harness and heater all measure correctly and 5E persists, because the remaining answer is a control board and that is worth a diagnosis rather than a guess. Call sooner if you are not comfortable taking the rear evaporator panel off with the defrost heater wiring behind it, which is a mains-voltage component in a compartment you have just filled with meltwater. Call urgently, and stop your own work, if both compartments are warm and the compressor runs constantly with a coil that never gets cold, because that is the sealed refrigerant system and it is licensed work. On an older fridge, get that quote before you spend anything else, since it is frequently the point at which replacing the appliance is the better decision.

faqs.q: What does 5E mean on a Samsung refrigerator?
faqs.a: The control cannot get a believable reading from a defrost temperature sensor, so it does not know when to start or stop a defrost cycle. The result is a coil that ices up and a compartment that stops holding temperature. The sensor is a small thermistor clipped to the evaporator behind a rear interior panel.

faqs.q: Is 5E the fridge sensor or the freezer sensor?
faqs.a: Published sources disagree, and some contradict themselves, so do not decide from the code. Look at where frost is building and which compartment is not holding temperature, then open that panel. The diagnosis and the part are the same either way, and the observation takes a minute while arguing about the code solves nothing.

faqs.q: Is 5E the same as SE or 5C?
faqs.a: SE and 5E are the same code, because on a seven-segment display the numeral 5 and a capital S are the same glyph. 5C is also the same fault on newer models, since Samsung changed the refrigerator code suffix from E to C partway through the range. Worth searching all three when looking for model-specific guidance.

faqs.q: Is 5E on my fridge the same as 5E on my Samsung washer?
faqs.a: No, and the overlap is pure coincidence. On a Samsung washing machine 5E is a drain fault, meaning water will not pump out. On a refrigerator it is a defrost sensor fault. They share nothing but two characters, so do not apply washer guidance to a fridge or the other way round.

faqs.q: Can I still use the fridge with a 5E code?
faqs.a: Only briefly, and watch the temperatures. With defrost not running properly the coil ices over, airflow drops and the compartment gradually warms, so food safety degrades over days rather than hours. Move anything perishable if a thermometer shows the fridge above its normal range, and get the repair done rather than living with it.

faqs.q: How do I test the sensor without a resistance chart for my model?
faqs.a: Measure across its two leads cold and write the number down, then warm the sensor in your closed hand for a minute and measure again. It is a thermistor, so the resistance should fall noticeably as it warms. A reading that does not move, or that shows open or a dead short, condemns it without needing any chart.

faqs.q: Why is there a solid block of ice behind the back panel?
faqs.a: Because defrost has not been running, which is exactly what this code is reporting. Every cooling cycle lays down a little frost, and the defrost cycle is what clears it. With the sensor circuit faulty the control never runs that cycle properly, so months of frost accumulate into a block that chokes the airflow and warms the compartment.
